subtopic: EXPRESSIONS OF SYMPATHY ON NEW BRUNSWICK STORM DISASTER

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: EXPRESSIONS OF SYMPATHY ON NEW BRUNSWICK STORM DISASTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all Canadians have been shocked to learn of the disaster which occurred over the week end along the east coast of New Brunswick in the Miramichi area, when a sudden and violent siorm struck with ferocious intensity. While it is impossible to know exactly how many fishermen were at sea that night over the long coastline, reports indicate that probably 40 or 50 boats were involved carrying some 80 to 100 men. When the storm struck the R.C.A.F. search and rescue unit was immediately ordered into action and it is continuing to co-ordinate the search by boats and planes available from the R.C.A.F., the R.C.M.P. and the Department of Fisheries in that area.
The latest reports show that 13 bodies have been recovered, and it is feared that the death toll may well exceed 30. The search and rescue work will continue until all hope must be abandoned.
I know I speak for all members of the house when I ask them to join me in extending the deepest sympathy to all those who have been bereaved and have suffered loss in this terrible tragedy of the sea.

subtopic: EXPRESSIONS OF SYMPATHY ON NEW BRUNSWICK STORM DISASTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a heavy heart that I rise to join the Prime Minister and all other members of the house in expressing the deepest and most heartfelt sympathy to the fishermen and their families of my constituency in the loss of many loved ones. As the Prime Minister has pointed out, it was a very great tragedy, one that has struck to the very core of the small fishing areas of Miramichi bay. At the same time I should like to pay tribute, as I know the house would, to the deeds of heroism performed by the fishermen who survived. May I also pay tribute to the search and rescue people who are playing a valiant role 66968-9-316
in trying to locate bodies, and also any fishermen who may still be alive. I express this sympathy and appreciation on behalf of the constituents whom I represent. Practically all the fishing gear and boats that have been lost were the property of fishermen of my constituency.
I should like to read a telegram I received this morning. It is addressed to me at the House of Commons and reads as follows:
Disaster Saturday at Escuminac must be treated as urgent. Immediate action for assistance for families of victims and to assist those fishermen who survived but lost all equipment is urgently required.
The telegram is signed by Mr. Graham Crocker, a man well qualified to assess the situation and who has been closely connected with the salmon fishermen throughout the years. On that note I should like to appeal to the Prime Minister and the cabinet to render every assistance possible as quickly as they can to relieve the suffering these people are undergoing. I suggest to the Prime Minister that possibly something could be done under the Canadian disaster relief fund to bring some relief to these stricken fishermen.

subtopic: WORLD REFUGEE YEAR-STATEMENT ON CANADIAN PARTICIPATION

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: WORLD REFUGEE YEAR-STATEMENT ON CANADIAN PARTICIPATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that the United Nations general assembly decided at its 13th session last autumn to establish a world refugee year. Canada was one of the 59 countries which voted in support of this resolution, which urged countries to co-operate in promoting world refugee year as a practical means for securing assistance for refugees throughout the world.
I am sure all hon. members will welcome, as does the government, the opening of world refugee year which will begin in Canada on Sunday, June 28. About 40 countries will be participating in the program of world refugee year.
Throughout the world, in the United Kingdom, the United States, France, New Zealand and elsewhere, national voluntary committees for world refugee year have been established, and a Canadian committee for world refugee year has also been formed with headquarters in Toronto. This committee, composed of distinguished individuals and representatives of interested organizations, I understand, has as its objective the raising of funds from the public for refugee causes. On behalf of the government I should like to take this opportunity to wish the committee every success in its humanitarian endeavour.
The Canadian government has participated regularly in all the United Nations relief programs, and recently it has increased some of its contributions in the hope of hastening solutions where they are possible. There is the program of the United Nations high commissioner for refugees, who has under his
IMr. Brooks.]

mandate 135,000 refugees in Europe who are still not settled 14 years after the close of world war II. Over 25,000 of these refugees are living in camps in conditions which render still more urgent their need for social and spiritual rehabilitation. As you know, this government has increased this year's contribution to the high commissioner to the level of $290,000 to facilitate closing these camps.
Today there are almost a million refugees in the Middle East and almost another million are crowded into the tiny area of Hong Kong. However difficult it may be to foresee an early solution to these problems, it is necessary that these refugees be fed and housed and, above all, that their hopes be kept alive. As far as possible, these refugees must be helped to become self-sufficient, if only so they may be self-respecting.
As you know, the United Nations relief and works agency has been established for Palestine refugees in the Near East. In addition to our regular cash contribution of $500,000 annually this government has, in response to urgent appeals from the agency, contributed a total of $3 million worth of Canadian wheat flour to this agency in the last two years. I would also remind members of the 8,000 European refugees in China, whose pilgrimage to a new home began after the Russian revolution of 1917. New homes abroad have already been promised to many of these refugees, and only the necessary funds are needed to complete their tragic odyssey around the world. This house will soon be asked to approve a contribution of $60,000 to this program.
All in all, this government has contributed $1,650,000 in cash to United Nations refugee programs over the last two years, and a further $3 million worth of food. In addition, large quantities of dried skim milk have been made available free of charge for distribution abroad by voluntary relief agencies. Finally, I need hardly refer again to the hundreds of thousands of refugees who have been accepted by Canada as new citizens.
The Canadian government has given continuous attention to refugee problems. It is, therefore, particularly happy to welcome world refugee year as a means whereby every Canadian can be encouraged to play his part in helping these unfortunate people. We must accept the opening of this year as a challenge; a challenge to the government, to voluntary agencies and to the general public.
The government is now considering the special contributions which it will make to the program of world refugee year. We are giving particular attention to the possibility of a scheme whereby a limited number of tubercular cases might be admitted to

Canada, together with their dependants, and given treatment in Canadian institutions. Assisting these tubercular cases to be cured and to re-establish themselves would be a valuable contribution to the solution of that most difficult and most tragic of all refugee problems, the residual or so-called hardcore cases of handicapped persons. Such a scheme will, of course, call for close consultation with the provinces, which are responsible for the institutions which would receive the cases.
We shall also take advantage of the summer recess to examine what further financial contributions might be made to the refugee effort. Members of this house can likewise play a useful role. I am sure they will join with me now in welcoming the inauguration of world refugee year. In particular we welcome the formation of the Canadian committee for world refugee year as a spontaneous public response to this important challenge.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that all members of the house welcome the general statement which the Secretary of State for External Affairs has just made. As he has observed, Canada should support the action taken at the United Nations to mark this year as world refugee year, thereby calling the attention of its members and of the peoples of the world generally to this hard-core problem of refugees. It will be remembered that at the end of the war Canada took a very active part and a highly important initiative in the formation of the international refugee organization, so that from the beginning it could be said that this country has demonstrated its interest in a problem that touches humanity and all nations.
In marking this refugee year I think it also desirable that we should determine to liquidate this problem for all time. The minister has noted that a national voluntary committee has been set up with headquarters in the city of Toronto. The Secretary of State for External Affairs will not take it amiss if I say that it may be necessary, as indeed he himself in the concluding part of his observations has indicated, to do more than set up a national voluntary committee. That committee will likely require the active support of the government of Canada. As he has suggested, one of the ways by which this could effectively be done would be to permit the entry into Canada of some of these stateless and homeless people who have been the victims of the policies of certain governments in alienating them from their homes and confronting them with the misery which has been theirs now for such a long time.

The minister also mentioned the Palestine refugees, some 1 million in number, whose welfare has been provided for again by the United Nations through the United Nations works and relief agency, operating as it does in Jordan and in the Gaza strip, to mention two chief areas of their work, an organization which Canada has supported with great devotion and with a sense of responsibility. It is significant that the work of UNWRA comes to the end of its formal assignment in 1960. While the minister did not indicate it, I am sure the government of Canada will give consideration to the prolongation of this work if that agency is regarded at the time as the most effective instrument for dealing with this additional serious problem.
The minister indicated that one of the gestures and one of the constructive proposals to which the government is giving consideration in co-operation with the provinces, who have the primary responsibility in this matter, is allowing the entry of tubercular refugees. In view of the fact that the government of Canada does contribute very large sums of money by way of assistance in tuberculosis control the interest of the government in this matter is understandable. I think it would also be important to recognize that apart altogether from the admission of individuals suffering from tuberculosis, consideration might be given in the name of humanity itself to the admission of some of these refugees who do not have this particular disability. In that connection I am sure the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration will give consideration to the fact that many of these people for many reasons could not qualify for admittance on the usual grounds now prescribed in the existing regulations and orders in council.
The government has said it will give consideration to helping financially to try to resolve this hard-core group of refugees. That, I think, is a consideration. More particularly it is a consideration which will be followed by an act that I am sure will meet with ready response on the part of the Canadian people, recognizing that in this way the people and the government of Canada are making their contributions to a problem that in the final analysis can only be resolved by collective effort.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether he has any statement to make to the house on what we all hope is the temporary break-up of the foreign ministers' conference at Geneva.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs; Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. Hon. members will have seen from the press that the foreign ministers' conference in Geneva has been adjourned until July 13. I point out that it has not broken up, as the Leader of the Opposition suggested. Since the proceedings have been fully reported in the press I shall not review the six weeks' conference in detail.
In my opinion, in assessing the position today the interval should not be regarded as a period of crisis but as an opportunity for re-examination of the position. As the foreign ministers of France, the United Kingdom and the United States pointed out in the statement they issued at the conclusion of the conference, this interval will give the Soviet government the opportunity of considering the western proposals further, and will give the western governments the opportunity to consider the position, particularly in relation to Mr. Khrushchev's Moscow speech of June 19. That pronouncement of the Soviet leader was not encouraging. He reiterated his demand for a peace treaty with the two parts of Germany, a procedure which would further hinder reunification, and he also proposed a time limit on efforts to achieve an agreed solution of the Berlin problem. In so doing he again stated that the Soviet union would sign a separate peace treaty with East Germany, with implied termination of western occupation rights, if agreement had not been reached on the Berlin problem at the end of that time.
At the time of recess the Soviet government had before it the offer of the western

powers to make certain modifications in the Berlin situation to meet the concerns expressed by the Soviet union. These included limitations on the strength and armament of the armed forces stationed there and the suggestion that reductions could be made; the formation of a four-power commission to settle disputes on rights of access; the possibility that without prejudice to existing responsibilities, procedures relating to access could be carried out by German personnel; and finally, measures to avoid in both parts of Berlin activities which might be disturbing to the other side.
The Canadian government commends the willingness the western powers have thus shown to accept adjustments in the existing arrangements while at the same time making clear their determination not to abandon western rights or forsake the people of West Berlin. Hon. members will have noticed in the press last week reports of the speech which the right hon. Prime Minister made in Princeton, in which he reiterated the view of the Canadian government that in this thermonuclear age differences between east and west must be resolved by negotiation. It has been with satisfaction that the Canadian government has watched the patient and determined efforts of the three western powers at Geneva to find some acceptable basis for continuing the negotiations, and it is gratifying that an early and fixed date has been selected for resumption of the foreign ministers' conference.
Whether on the resumption of the conference it will be found that there is a suitable foundation for a continuation of the negotiations will depend largely on the attitude of the Soviet union. As to the possibility of the heads of government meeting taking place, it is too soon to say whether it is likely that such a meeting will be held. The negotiations so far have served to demonstrate to the Soviet union that the western powers are serious, determined and united on the question of Berlin, but it is the view of this government that the search must be continued for a framework within which a settlement can be reached. We should not be turned aside from this search or deflected from our purpose and policy by provocative statements from the other side. It is possible that an intensive re-examination by the western powers of what the Soviet representative said during the conference, both in private sessions as well as in the plenary meetings, will reveal certain points that could be usefully pursued.
The Canadian government is therefore prepared during the period of recess to participate in the examination of what has taken

Prime Minister in the house on April 7, 1959, when he stated that no agreement could be acceptable to the west which placed in jeopardy the security of Berlin, the freedom of its citizens, or which might have the effect of foreclosing the prospect of reunification of Germany.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Were there not also 10 million letters being delivered daily when the hon. minister was in the opposition and was critical of the Postmaster General of the day?

Yes, Mr. Speaker, there were, but I never asked the house any question calling for such particulars.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will not be surprised when I inform you, sir, that we

are proposing today an amendment to the motion to go into supply in order to deal with a subject matter which we attempted to put before the house earlier as a motion which we thought affected the privileges of the house.
On Friday last, Mr. Speaker, you stated, in the decision you gave at that time, that no barrier was being raised to the presentation of this matter on another occasion under different circumstances from those which governed the motion before you at that time. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, you suggested that the subject matter could be brought before the house on the next motion to go into supply. Normally this is not the kind of subject matter that should take up one of the six supply motions to which we are permitted to move amendments; but in these special circumstances, though we might have wished to put forward another and more general subject for discussion, we feel that we must deal with this particular matter. If the motion before you last Friday, which you decided could not be treated as one affecting privilege and should go on the order paper in the normal way, could have been dealt with in that form then it would not have been necessary to deal with it on a supply day. The Prime Minister did not find it possible to arrange for a discussion of the motion in that form, but he had second thoughts and suggested that the business of the house might be rearranged in order to deal with this matter on a supply motion today.
The notice of motion which I placed on the order paper earlier embodied certain affirmations contained in a judgment of the president of the Exchequer Court of Canada. It concluded with a request that a committee be established, or the committee on privileges and elections be used, to examine certain actions of the hon. member of this house mentioned in that judgment and that this committee, having looked into the question, should report whether the conduct mentioned in these findings was in accordance with the dignity of parliament.
That notice of motion, Mr. Speaker, accurately reflected in its terms certain affirmations contained in the judgment. No member on the government side has alleged that the notice of motion which we put on the order paper had in the slightest particular departed from the statements made and the conclusions drawn in this judicial document. As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, in your statement last Friday you recommended the notice of motion to the house as a fair and equitable summary of this judicial document, and I believe that is a good indication of the fair manner in which we have proceeded in our efforts to discuss this matter.

The conclusions in your ruling last Friday, Mr. Speaker, confirm our own view that we were on solid ground in arguing that the conduct of a member could be investigated on the basis of statements made about that conduct without the necessity of a member of this house preferring a specific charge, and that as a ground for presenting such a motion there was no need of charges specifically made, as argued by spokesmen on the government side. In this connection, Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer the house to a question which I addressed to you last Wednesday as to whether a question of privilege could be raised on allegations direct or implied in a judgment of a court in some other way.
The answer to my question, of course, was in the affirmative. Any other answer to that question, in your words, Mr. Speaker, to quote from your decision of last Friday at page 4930 of Hansard, would be "to overlook precedents in which inquiries have been undertaken on the basis of charges implied from documents". That surely must dispose of the arguments advanced by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice on this matter. Later it is stated in your decision, Mr. Speaker, and I quote again from page 4930, lines 29 to 33:
On the authorities it appears to be open to an hon. member to confront the house with charges against another member implicit in documents in the possession of the house, but in my view the charge must be there.
In other words, according to your decision, they must be implicit in the document. I am sure that conclusion is correct, but I still believe that this particular part of the procedural problem has been finally resolved, because no argument adduced from any source in this house has disposed of the precedents established in the Foster and Garland cases in the Canadian House of Commons and the Boothby case in the British house when charges were neither specifically made nor documents referred to.
Last Friday, Mr. Speaker, you placed on record in the house a sentence which seems to me to be of very great importance. It had to do with your attempt to formulate from the affirmations in the motion a possible charge which in your mind it was your duty to try to find, whether in fact such a charge, direct or implied, did exist. Your sentence on that point was as follows, and I quote from page 4931 of Hansard, lines 16 to 25:
If these observations or "affirmations", as they are styled in the notice of motion, are taken as fact-
In other words if they are taken as fact; and the government insists, as I will point out 66968-9-317
Malton Land Expropriation later, that we must take them as facts if we are going to produce this kind of motion. You went on, Mr. Speaker:
-and the worst construction is put on them, it would appear that the hon. member for Peel on behalf of his constituents unsuccessfully attempted to get more generous compensation for them from public funds for the lands which the crown had expropriated than they were warranted in receiving.
That formulation, Mr. Speaker, drawn from the affirmations in the notice of motion-and I am certainly not complaining about it or questioning it in any way-goes further than any statement made by any hon. member on this side of the house.
Will the hon. member permit a question at this stage? Should the hon. member not read the next sentence, "This summary does not do justice either way"?

I do not think that has any bearing at all on what I have said. Earlier in your remarks, Mr. Speaker, you stated that no close precedent was cited and that you were unable to find any. Based on the construction that such conduct as was referred to in the judgment of the court which was mentioned in the notice of motion had not in the past been punished and that no close precedent was cited, you thereby ruled that a question of the privilege of the house was not prima facie involved. That is the ruling of the Chair and it has been confirmed by a decision of the house. Naturally, Mr. Speaker, all members are bound to accept it even though they may, not be convinced that it is warranted by precedents of by the evidence. A decision has been made, and the house is bound by it.
I suggest that a decision of far-reaching importance was made in the ruling given last Friday. It seems to me to involve the answers to this question:	Can a member,
without any breach of the privileges of parliament, seek for his constituents funds from the public treasury which in the circumstances they are not warranted in having? When we raised that as a question, Mr. Speaker, for discussion on the estimates of the Department of Transport, the Minister of Transport merely replied by indulging in, if he will permit to call it such, a political tirade.
Now, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that this is the kind of question which could be more profitably discussed in the committee on privileges and elections. If it is to be discussed on a supply motion, if the debate on this matter is now to take a new turn, that is of course the result of the refusal of the government to permit that particular committee to inquire into the matter in a way
4996	HOUSE OF
Malton Land Expropriation which would ensure that all the tacts were known as they concern the two members of parliament involved, the Minister of Transport and the hon. member for Peel, and to examine into this matter so the right conclusions might be drawn from the facts discovered. Such a committee would not have been packed against the government and could have checked on certain statements and assertions included in a court finding, not an alleged finding, which certainly appeared to have reflected on members of parliament, some of which statements have been contradicted outside the court.
The Prime Minister dismisses this as of little significance unless on his own responsibility a member of parliament is willing to accept all these statements and assertions as true, which would mean that he would presumably have to accept the statements contradicting them outside the court as untrue.

That is a pretty thin
argument.

It may be a thin argument
to the Prime Minister, but it is a pretty impressive argument to anybody who approaches this matter in an objective manner.
Witnesses, such as the Minister of Transport, who did not appear before the court could have been called before such a committee. I submit parliament would not be acting as a court in such an inquiry, and 1 submit also there would have been no trial. There would have been an attempt, with witnesses called, to check certain statements made under oath in a court which reflected on the propriety, so we thought, of the conduct of a member of this house.
If one says that no member should have to submit to investigation or inquiry by the House of Commons or a committee of the house of statements into his conduct in a matter of public business until he has been charged with an offence, then I say that is disproven by many precedents. Furthermore, in this case the investigation would have been into statements made about a member in a court under oath, statements made in the evidence which the judge reported in his findings, some of which were denied or contradicted later outside the court. Is that not something which should be inquired into? I hope to produce enough evidence, Mr. Speaker, to convince members that the answer to that question must be yes.
Yet it has been said that unless in these findings there is an explicit charge with which a member is willing to identify himself by repeating it in this house, there can be no such parliamentary inquiry. The fact that


this argument is wrong and without any logical foundation is shown by the statement that if the member concerned or the Minister of Transport had moved a motion of inquiry into these assertions, it would have been accepted by the government without any argument. However, this procedure of inquiry by the committee on privileges and elections we thought was fair to everyone concerned. This procedure has, up to the present, been rejected by the Prime Minister, who has justified his rejection by accusing those of us who are proposing it of McCarthyism. This merely shows the weakness of the case, as all smokescreen diversions do, whether by the Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice or the Minister of Transport.
At this time, Mr. Speaker, it becomes necessary not to see whether the privileges of parliament are involved, because you have decided they are not, but to look into the conduct of the Minister of Transport and the hon. member for Peel and the government in the handling of this whole question of the Malton expropriations. The evidence we have in that matter is in the findings of the president of the Exchequer Court of Canada; in statements made by those concerned or some of those concerned outside of the house, and in the words of the Minister of Transport inside the house. We have had no word as yet from the hon. member for Peel inside the house, but some remarks have been made by him outside, at least as reported in the press. Surely, Mr. Speaker, today he will have something to say about this matter, even at this late date.
I must emphasize that the observations and statements about which I am talking, the statements that to us seem to reflect on somebody's conduct, are not made by me. They are made in the findings of a court judgment which I found it my duty to repeat as bearing on this problem. The Prime Minister, I repeat, takes the position that there can be no inquiry into these findings by a committee of this house concerned with parliamentary privileges unless a member takes the responsibility for accepting all those findings of the court as true, and therefore something on which a charge could and must be laid by a member of parliament. He argues that one must also accept responsibility for the comments on these statements made by others, including the member for Peel himself and the Minister of Transport, which contradict certain of these statements in the findings of the court.
Then he says that parliament should not investigate them, whether or not they appear to reflect on a member. Whatever statement
7 MAI 1959
is made outside the house, in a court of law or in some other place, which reflects on the conduct of a member-that has nothing to do with the privileges of the house unless you accept it as true and lay charges based on it. That is the government's position, and it is a very strange position indeed. I could think of some adjectives used by the Minister of Justice the other day which might be appropriate in describing it, but I will not do that. However, I will say this; that I consider the position a travesty of respect for parliamentary rights and privileges. Perhaps it is an effective method of avoiding any inquiry by the men who talk about McCarthyism because we will not condemn a person before such an inquiry is made to find out the facts.
The Prime Minister laughs; he finds this amusing.
I find such arguments or lack of arguments amusing.
After the arguments you advanced last week?

What are these statements in a finding of a court which reflect on a member and which should be examined in fairness to the member himself and corrected if they are wrong or misleading? If that is not done -and the government has certainly not made it possible yet-they remain on the record of the court and indeed, in view of the discussion we have had in this house, on the record of parliament.
Does the member concerned wish that to happen? Does the Prime Minister wish that to happen, namely that the court record go unchallenged and unexamined? Does the Minister of Transport, who is so directly concerned with all this, wish that to happen? No doubt he will be taking part in this debate. Perhaps I might be permitted to address a few questions to him. May I ask him first this question. Why did he not appear in order to clear these matters up when these statements were made before the court?
Mr Hees: May I answer that question right now. The answer is that I was never summoned or asked to appear.
Naturally; I expected that would be the minister's reply.
It is true.

The minister knew that the business of his department was being considered by this court. The minister must have known of some of the statements that were being made in this case. He is the Minister of Transport. This was a case which concerned his department. In view of the 66968-9-317J
Malton Land Expropriation statements that were made, which were confusing, which were contradictory, and which affected him directly, did the minister not think-notwithstanding the fact that he had not been subpoenaed-it might have been a good thing to go to court and clear this matter up?
I have answered every one of those questions in this house posed by you.
The minister will have a chance. The minister said he had answered all the questions.
I have answered the questions you put to me.

Let us see. What are these statements, these allegations, some of which remain unchallenged in the court findings and are now on the records of parliament? The minister will be glad to follow this because he will no doubt want to deal with some of them. All my statements are based on the document.
In the first place, it was stated under oath that the member for Peel sought to bind the treasury in advance to accept an increased valuation of certain properties which were being expropriated and which had already been valued, according to the minister, on approximately six other occasions by departmental and other valuators, and which were the outstanding claims after 180 others had been settled.
The member for Peel himself stated under oath that the department had in fact accepted his proposal for such an additional valuation by an appraiser to be recommended by him, which valuation would be binding on the owners and on the crown. There was considerable evidence on this point, which I now propose to put on the record.
The minister had written the member for Peel on July 19, 1957 that his department had thought the appraisals "fair and reasonable"-those were the words he used-after six earlier valuations. These are the appraisals of the eleven outstanding parcels of property in these Malton expropriations. He had thought that the appraisals, after six earlier valuations, were fair and reasonable. He stated that the Department of Veterans Affairs, which was concerned in these cases since some of the owners were veterans, concurred in that view. He pointed out that there was a test case, the Hatton case, before the exchequer court which would provide a basis for any further settlement, he thought. He has added that it would be well, in his opinion, to wait for this to be settled first; otherwise-and I quote from his communication-
4998	HOUSE OF
Mdlton Land Expropriation
-the department could be accused of being wasteful of the taxpayers' money by giving in to unreasonable demands.
In his letter of July 19 the minister went on to say this:
I would not like to commit myself at this stage to arbitration in the sense of appointing an independent appraiser acceptable to both the veterans and ourselves.
But he added-and I quote from his letter:
X would certainly be prepared to consider this possibility further if the veterans were prepared to agree by contract in advance that the report of such an independent appraiser was final and binding on them.
That is from the minister's letter. So the member for Peel, relying on this willingness to consider the matter further, began to act as he thought-and no doubt quite sincerely thought-in the interests of his constituents. On July 24, 1959 he wrote the minister that the owners, and I quote from that letter-
-have agreed to the matter being arbitrated by a single arbitrator to be agreed upon between yourself and themselves.
If words mean anything, they mean that the owners had agreed to an arbitrator whose decision would be binding on both parties. There is no doubt on that score, as I shall now try to point out from further communications. The member in this letter added that he would submit the name of such an arbitrator for the minister's consideration. The name recommended and accepted by the minister was Mr. Earl Clare.
The member for Peel then had a meeting with the owners some time in August, according to the evidence. Again from the evidence, on page 4, he told the owners of a talk with the minister and of the plan he had proposed to the minister for an independent valuator who-and I quote the words of the finding-"would be a reputable and reliable real estate man". The member asked the owners, according to the findings, to accept this proposal for an arbitrator whose decision would be binding-and again I quote from the finding-"on both the owners and the department". When the owners agreed, the member for Peel wrote to the assistant deputy minister of transport on August 27-and this appears on page 4 of the finding-confirmed that the owners would accept an arbitration by a new valuator- and I quote again-"whose finding shall be binding on both parties". There is no misunderstanding there. That language is perfectly clear. There is no room for misunderstanding as to what that language could possibly mean other than there should be an arbitration binding on both sides.
Would the hon. member mind my asking him a question?
No.
Who wrote that last letter?
The member wrote it to the minister.
The hon. member for Peel wrote it?
That is right.
But so far, there is no agreement of any kind under which the department agreed to be bound in any way, shape or form.

I shall come to that matter in due course. On August 29 the assistant deputy minister of transport wrote to the member for Peel that after discussion with the officials of treasury board and the Department of Justice, I think it was, he felt that arbitration of the kind suggested in the member's letter was impracticable; that it was contrary to the intention of the Expropriation Act for the government to be bound in advance in the manner suggested by the member for Peel; that it would establish a precedent which could have-and I quote-"extremely serious and dangerous consequences for the future"; and that the court was better qualified than an arbitrator to come to a sound decision.
Then occurred a meeting between the minister and the member in the Hunter building on September 19. Mr. Booth, the assistant deputy minister of transport, was present for the first part of the meeting but was not present for the last part of it. On page 5 of the findings it is reported that the member for Peel again-and I quote from the findings on page 5-
-suggested that an independent appraiser should he appointed and that both the crown and the owners should be bound by his valuations.
On this occasion the assistant deputy minister pointed out that, as recommendations were subject to the approval of treasury board, the minister could not be bound in advance by any new valuation. I am glad to put that on record. The assistant deputy minister also stated that the department was satisfied with the valuations that had been made and that they were valid. There was further discussion between the minister and member after the assistant deputy minister left, and there is no record of any kind of that discussion, as far as I know, in the finding of the court or anywhere else. But after that discussion on October 1, 1957 the minister wrote to the member for Peel, and I quote from his letter of October 1:
My understanding of your proposal-
That is the proposal of the member.

-was that if new proposals were made by a valuator acceptable to you the owners in question would agree to be bound by his valuation.
That is the owners in question. That surely does not make any sense unless the arrangements bound the government as well.
Oh, oh.

It is quite simple to show that, and it is even easier to show that that was the impression in the hon. member's mind. I have lots of evidence to prove that.
The hon. member had every right to assume that the obligation was on both sides. How otherwise could he have got the owners to accept such an obligation? What could they possibly have gained by signing such a one sided agreement? I cannot believe that the hon. member after his talk with the minister would have put it forward to them in such one sided terms. There is evidence taken under oath to show that the understanding of the hon. member was perfectly clear on this matter, that there was no doubt in his mind as to what had happened. Let me quote from this letter of October 1. In it the minister asked for:
-the written undertakings of the owners to be bound by Mr. Clare's valuations. When these valuations are received I will proceed along the lines indicated to you-
That is, to the member. I continue:
-in our discussion.
Mr. Speaker, what were the lines under which they were to proceed and which were mentioned by the hon. member in the letter of October 1?
Would the hon. member like an answer to that question right now?
I have it from the documents.
Do you want an answer? You have asked a question and I am prepared to answer it right now. If you do not want the answer-and I do not think you do-I will not, of course, give it.
Mr. Speaker, I have an answer to that question not from the intervention of the minister but from the documents in this matter-
You do not want me to answer.

I say there was a sharp conflict of evidence here. A couple of weeks ago the Prime Minister of course could not find any conflicts or contradictions in the evidence at all. I maintain that this is a sharp conflict of evidence. The findings of the court are very clear as to what the hon. member said in the court under oath. I will read what is
Malton Land Expropriation found at page 7 of the findings of the president of the Exchequer Court of Canada:
When Mr. Pallett was asked what lines had been indicated to him in the discussion, his answer was-
I quote from his answer taken from the findings:
-"whatever valuations were made by the independent valuator would be accepted by the Department of Transport".
What has the minister got to say about that?
Do you want me to answer that?
I asked you a question and I will give you an opportunity to answer it.

I shall be very glad to do so. The agreement between the hon. member for Peel and myself, as I outlined to him in my office, was that we would be perfectly willing to appoint an independent valuator, Mr. Clare, and that when his valuations were received they would be submitted to the treasury board staff for examination. That was the agreement.

That is the minister's answer, so I will read again what the hon. member for Peel said under oath before the court:
-whatever valuations were made by the independent valuator would be accepted by the Department of Transport.
Let us examine what the assistant deputy minister said about this when he was questioned on it. I quote again from the evidence. Mr. Booth said:
The minister did not say that.
The findings then add this:
Mr. Pallett said that he had convinced the minister and that he left the meeting with the understanding that the valuation made by Mr. Clare-would bind both the department and the owners and that it was his responsibility to get the owners' signatures on documents agreeing to his valuation.
Those words are found at page 7 of the findings. Mr. Booth intervened to try to correct the impression of the hon. member for Peel that he had a proposal accepted by the minister.
Read the next portion. It is all part of the same thing.
I have some more to read from page 7.
Just read this to conclude that paragraph.

Yes, I will be very glad to read it:
There was thus a sharp difference between the evidence of Mr. Booth and of Mr. Pallett-

Malton Land Expropriation
I am reading from page 7 of the findings. I continue:
Mr. Pallett said that he had convinced the minister and that he left the meeting with the understanding that the valuation to be made by Mr. Clare, if he was found to be qualified-
I left that out because it did not seem to me to be pertinent. I continue:
-would bind both the department and the owners and that it was his responsibility to get the owners' signatures on documents agreeing to his valuation. But Mr. Booth was clear that the minister was most anxious to settle the matter and do everything possible short of binding the crown in advance of the proposed valuation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, short of binding the crown.
Carry on.

Of course that is the position the assistant deputy minister took. He said his minister was not bound by the valuation. But the hon. member for Peel, a member of this house, said he left the meeting with the understanding that it would bind both the government and the owners and that it was his responsibility to get the owners' signatures. If there was this misunderstanding between the hon. member for Peel and Mr. Booth on this matter-and there obviously was-why did the minister not clear up the misunderstanding and put the hon. member for Peel right?
On the basis of the documents I have read it seems to me that the position taken by the hon. member for Peel was perfectly reasonable. Why else would the hon. member try to secure the signatures? Why should he have been put in such a false position by the minister if the situation were otherwise? Why should he be asked to get signatures of the owners on the ground that they would accept the valuations of the independent appraiser if the government was not going to be bound by the valuations?
Do you want an answer to that?

Why would the minister ask these people through the hon. member for Peel, to accept a one sided valuation of that kind? I suggest that the hon. member had no intention of asking that at all, and that he was completely honest and sincere when he said that he believed these valuations would bind both the government and the owners. That is what he said before the court.
Would you like an answer to that question? I am prepared to answer that question if you wish. I do not believe you want any answer.
The minister is just trying to destroy the argument of the Leader of the Opposition.
I have already answered the questions the minister speaks of from the documents before me. The minister will have lots of opportunity to make reference to this. He can speak in this debate.
I asked you a question. You seem to be genuinely asking for information. Do you want an answer to your question? Do you wish me to reply to your question?
I have the answer.
No, you have not. You do not want the answer.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The minister will know that the hon. member who has the floor wants an answer when he sits down and gives the minister an opportunity to speak.

This is very interesting, in view of the minister's intervention. On October 3 the hon. member for Peel wrote the minister saying that he would send along the signed forms of the owners in the form of an agreement between the owners and the government. What kind of agreement would that have been which bound only the owners and had no binding effect whatever on the government? The minister replied on October 7, and I quote from his letter on that occasion:
I have been advised that barring unforeseen difficulties we shall be able to complete the formalities within this time limit and under the circumstances I agree to proceeding in the manner you have arranged.
There was a suggested time limit of two months. The minister on October 7 said he would agree to proceeding in the manner arranged by the hon. member for Peel. We know what the hon. member for Peel thought he was doing, because he said under oath in court what he thought he was doing. There was nothing in that letter of October 3, after these talks, to warn the hon. member that the valuation was not binding on the government but was binding only on the owners. There was nothing in that letter of October 7 to clear up any misunderstanding which obviously was in the hon. member's mind or he obviously would not have made the statements he did before the court.
The following is also an answer to the minister's interruption. On page 8 of the findings we find the following:
It was Mr. Pallett's opinion that what was meant was that the valuation would be acceptable to both parties.
That was three times in these findings that the hon. member's views of this matter had been set down in black and white as implying an arrangement, a proposal, an agreement -whatever you want to call it-which was binding both on the government and on the owners.
Would the hon. member read again that paragraph, the next words on page 8?

I will be glad to as the Prime Minister seems very curious. I should have read the whole document, Mr. Speaker. I am now reading from the evidence itself:
On October 7, 1957, the minister wrote to Mr. Pallett acknowledging receipt ol his letter of October 3, 1957, and referring to Mr. Booth's telephone conversation with Mr. Pallett commenting on the shortness of the two months' limit and concluding as follows:
"I have been advised that barring unforeseen difficulties we shall be able to complete the formalities within this time limit, and under the circumstances X agree to proceeding in the manner you have arranged."
There was controversy over the meaning of the last portion of this letter, "I agree to proceeding in the manner you have arranged." It was Mr. Pallett's opinion that what was meant was that Mr. Clare would do the valuation and that it would be acceptable to both parties. But Mr. Booth, who had prepared the letter for the Minister's signature, said the phrase "formalities" meant simply the formalities in the case of agreed settlement including submissions to the treasury board.
For the benefit of the Prime Minister I might say I was coming to that in my statement.
My hon. friend always seems to be coming to it but never does.
Oh, oh.

The Prime Minister obviously wants it to be on the record twice and I will be glad to oblige. The Prime Minister is very anxious to show that a civil servant is really the determining influence in this matter and that the civil servant was instructing the member.
It is clear-and this is a very important part of the evidence-that Mr. Pallett knew the need for approval of the treasury board when he stated that the minister said that he would have to take the responsibility. He would take the responsibility of dealing with the treasury board. If as the assistant deputy minister argued-and the Prime Minister is so anxious to get the assistant deputy minister's argument on the record-"formalities" meant simply the formalities in the case of agreed settlements including submissions to the treasury board, why did the minister not make this clear to the member and later to the court? Why allow what he admits was a misunderstanding to persist? According to the hon. member for Peel the minister stated that he would take the responsibility in connection with the approval of treasury board. Is that an accurate statement? Are we to accept that statement as such, that the minister would take the responsibility of dealing with treasury board with regard to these evaluations? There is some evidence
Malton Land Expropriation to support that interpretation, Mr. Speaker; but why did not the minister-and I ask him again even though he was not subpoenaed-appear in the court and clear this whole matter up? Why leave the matter there in the way it was left in the hon. member's mind? There is no doubt what the hon. member thought was going on. Surely it is not a very fair way for the minister to treat the hon. member, to leave him under what he admits now to have been a very serious misapprehension, a misapprehension so clear that he the minister, refers to it in this house.
Mr. Speaker, let us just see what the minister had to say about this in parliament. On June 9, as reported on pages 4457 and 4458 of Hansard, he dealt with this matter in reply to some questions from the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier). He said first of all that he would not comment on the findings of the court. I would ask the minister, and he can reply to this question when he gets up to speak, why would he not comment on the findings? Again on page 4530 he said it would be inappropriate for him to discuss the judgment and he would not do so. On page 4591 he merely accepts the decision of the court with regard to the payment to be made, and that is all. The minister would not comment on the findings of the court, but presumably he expects us to accept as true and accurate those findings; otherwise we would not have been asked to base a specific charge on them. The minister would not comment, but he said that we were to accept them all as true and accurate if we are going to base a charge and to request a committee to inquire into it.
When did I say that, Mr. Speaker?

The position of the government, goodness knows, is surely clear enough on this matter. The position of the government is that there can be no inquiry into this matter on a question of privilege unless some member on this side of the house takes the responsibility of identifying himself with all these findings and specific charges, and therefore assumes that they are accurate and true. However, I do not believe the hon. member has removed all the doubts that are in our minds. He said he thanks the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) for at last bringing this matter up in a fashion which has permitted him to speak in this house. Here we have a situation involving two hon. members of this house. The Minister of Transport has said one thing here in the house on his responsibility as a minister of the crown, and the hon. member for Peel has stated the precise opposite under oath in one of the high courts of the country. This has to do with something of real importance. This concerns the disbursement of money out of the treasury of the country. That is what is at issue, and it is not a trivial matter at all. I am not certain of the amount involved but I am told that the amount in all of these cases would probably be about $50,000. I must say that personally I do not regard $50,000 as a trivial sum at any time,
Malton Land Expropriation and although some hon. members of this house may view an amount of this nature in a different light, it is not the amount that is important but rather the principle that is involved.
This was a question of the protection of the treasury on the one hand, against the interests of a group of constituents on the other. It seems to me that the House of Commons, which has the duty of protecting the taxpayers' money above all its other duties, is entitled to have a conflict of this kind resolved in no uncertain fashion.

I am told that appraisers do not work for free. I have not looked up the record to see precisely what this gentleman was paid but he certainly was paid some of the taxpayers' money and that, to us, obviously was wasted. It was wasted because these appraisals were of no value. Not only was it wasted but it had the effect of resulting in litigation of a character which may have cost the taxpayers even more.
But what I ask myself is, what did the minister think he was accomplishing by appointing this appraiser? What did he think this appraiser was going to do? Did the minister for one minute think that if these appraisals were higher than the other appraisals on which the department had already settled he could recommend that the department and the treasury board should accept and pay larger sums to these owners on a voluntary basis than had been paid to other people in similar circumstances? Did the minister really think that the government of Canada could treat citizens in that fashion? I suggest that it is almost preposterous to suggest such a thing. That these people could have gone into the courts and taken their chances and perhaps have got more than other people who settled voluntarily is one thing, but that the government of its own motion should make fish of one and fowl of another is surely a preposterous idea. It seems to me the house is entitled to know what was the purpose of appointing this appraiser, what it was expected to accomplish and what would be accomplished.
Now I come to the other question of whether or not the appraiser was instructed. On that of course, I do not intend to quarrel with the hon. member for Peel. The hon. member for Peel has said that the witness who gave evidence in the court gave evidence which was not true. The hon. member is a member of this house and he said that on his responsibility as a member of this house, and I accept it without question at all. But that does raise another question. However, I have a cutting here from the Regina Leader-Post of June 18, 1959, which quotes the executive director of the appraisal institute of Canada as follows:

-in Regina Thursday the land appraiser involved in the House of Commons hassle over land in the Toronto area is not a qualified appraiser.

I am not going to make any more of that except to bring it before the house as another bit of uncontradicted evidence that the committee we are asking to have set up should resolve.
The other point I want to make, which seems to me to be perhaps the only other point I can usefully make, is this. The hon. member for Peel while he was a private member, as he himself has said, undertook to further what he conceived to be the legitimate interests of a group of his constituents. In doing so, because there was what he and the minister both called a misunderstanding between him and the minister, he led those constituents to believe-he did not deny this; in fact he admitted it quite openly-that he had on their behalf reached an agreement with the minister that the government as well as the owners would be bound by this appraisal. In other words, far from helping these constituents he in fact, if I may use a popular expression, led them down the garden path. I do not for a minute suggest that he intended to but that is what happened. These people, or at least one of them, were put-did the minister wish to ask a question?

speechtext: What about the extra $2,000 by which the award was increased? It is not a negligible amount.
I have not forgotten about that at all. It seems to me that if the exchequer court was going to allow an extra $1,000-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Two thousand.

-$2,000; if these people were not satisfied to accept the same kind of settlement which had been arrived at with the other people, the exchequer court would probably have allowed that much in any event. It may be that there could have been a settlement without any action, and that was indicated before action was taken, as is shown in the judgment. The department felt that this $11,200 was open for acceptance before action was taken, and indeed it was the offer on which the learned judge based his judgment. Therefore, if this litigant had known for sure and been given an unqualified assurance of what the minister is telling us now, namely that there was a misunderstanding between the hon. member and the minister, it seems highly

improbable that any such action would have been taken, because this action was taken, as hon. members know, by a leading counsel in the city of Toronto, an eminent member of the bar who I have personal reason to know has been not unsuccessful in actions against the crown. It is very unlikely that a conscientious and able counsel would have advised his client to enter into an action if he had been advised in advance by the hon. member for Peel that there had been a misunderstanding and that no such agreement existed.
It seems to me that that comes right back to what I have said from the start is the nub of this case, that this litigant was allowed to go into court believing, and having every reason to believe, because she had been so assured by the hon. member for Peel-and we have no evidence that she was ever told the contrary-that an agreement had been made between the minister and the hon. member for Peel of the character that the hon. member for Peel said under oath existed. It seems to me that whether or not this matter be a question of privilege-and while we submit to Your Honour's ruling, it is very hard sometimes to submit-there can be no question of the impropriety in the first place of appointing an appraiser to perform no function that we have been told about that could be useful; to spend public money on this appraisal that could not possibly have the effect that those agreed in advance to be bound by it believed it would have.
There is also the contradiction between the statement of a minister of the crown, a member of this house, and another member of this house who today occupies the high and honourable position of chief government whip. I therefore submit, that the government-and the Prime Minister owes it to the house-should bring this matter before a committee and have it cleared up.
Before I resume my seat, if I have any more time, I should like to remind hon. members that in the year 1953, not long before I became a member of this house, another case arose in which the name of an hon. member sitting on the government side of the house was brought into question, not in the house at all, not in a judgment of a court, but by some articles in a Toronto newspaper. What happened in that case?

You had better give the facts.

The Prime Minister says I had better give the facts. I have given all the facts that I intend to give about that case. If the Prime Minister wants to supplement the facts he is perfectly welcome to do so because there were no other facts that I know about. There were insinuations in the article in the newspaper, and I am not going to repeat those insinuations at all. There were insinuations affecting the conduct of a member in his relations with someone who had a contract with the government, but not affecting his relations with the government; affecting his relations with a contractor who had one or several contracts with the government.
What happened in that case? The hon. member in question came into the house of his own motion. I searched Hansard quite diligently and I have not found any reference made by any other hon. member to that hon. member's connection with the matter until he came into the house, or indeed afterwards, so far as that goes. He came into the house of his own motion made a statement very similar to the statement made today by the hon. member for Peel, in which he stated on his honour that he had no kind of improper connections whatsoever that affected him as a member and he put his seat in jeopardy. That is what happened in that case.
I do not say for a minute that the hon. member for Peel should have put his seat in jeopardy; I am not making any such suggestion. But I am saying that what he should have done at the very beginning of this matter-and I come back to this again -is to have come into this house at once and explained to hon. members in the frank way he did today precisely what had happened. He did not need to ask for an investigation. There is no compulsion on him to do that. My hon. friend from Laurier did not ask for an investigation the other day. He simply got up and stated the facts, and that was the end of the matter.
There was another occasion, of course, in that parliament before I became a member of parliament-the Prime Minister will remember it very well-when the leader of the opposition made insinuations and charges and more about a very distinguished member of the government, and that member of the government on two different occasions took immediate advantage of the first possible opportunity to reply to those insinuations. There is nothing new about it. What is new about this is that the hon. member for Peel did nothing about it for all this long period of time. Why, it is hard to understand. It is very hard to understand why now. What is

Malton Land Expropriation even harder to understand, what is even more difficult to reconcile with the proprieties, is that the Minister of Transport, having read in a judgment of a high court that a member of this house, the chief whip of his own party, had said under oath that he had made an agreement of a certain character with the minister, should not have undertaken action on his own and at once to explain what the real facts were. The minister still has not told us when he told the hon. member for Peel about this misunderstanding, nor when he told the other persons involved about the situation. There are still many unanswered questions about this matter and it is to resolve those questions which still affect the word given by a member under oath in a court, and the word given on his responsibility as a minister by a minister of the crown here in this house, that we believe this motion should pass.

Mr. Speaker, the reason that prompted me to take part in this debate is more than anything else-and I wish to emphasize this fact -the extraordinary and, as a matter of fact, the very revealing attitude that the government and the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) adopted in dealing with this matter ever since it has been brought into the house. Indeed, it is because of the attitude of the Prime Minister that the house and parliament are forced to make an investigation into a matter which should have been brought before a special committee which might have studied this question far more fully than can be done in this House of Commons.
I consider as unparliamentary, irresponsible and unwise the fact that the Prime Minister did not of his own free will institute an investigation into this matter and offer some clarification of statements which are to be found in a judgment of the exchequer court in the Drew case. I submit, Mr. Speaker, it is absolutely contempt of parliament for the Prime Minister to refuse to institute a formal inquiry into the statements of the exchequer court which raises doubt not only as to the propriety of the role played by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Pallett) but which in fact imply that there may be some doubt as to how far the government, and particularly the Department of Transport, was committed and involved in negotiations or arrangements with persons concerned which, according to the judgment, were considered to be irregular.
I also submit that it was in a narrow and unjustifiable spirit that the Prime Minister attempted to place the opposition in the role of prosecutor and tried to force the opposition to make charges against the hon. member for Peel and to let us understand that


if we were not willing to make those charges then we should desist completely from trying to obtain some information or some clarification of this most dubious matter.
The opposition has, of course, cited many precedents where such inquiries as were asked for by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) were made without formal charges being laid, and yet the Prime Minister refuses to have an inquiry made on statements which throw confusion and doubt, not only on the hon. member for Peel but on the activities of parliament, in that it places members of parliament in an unfavourable light. As regretful as this fact may be, I am quite sure that no one in this house will deny that there is unfortunately a large number of people in Canada who feel that politics and politicians are not necessarily synonymous with objectivity and with honesty.
Leaving the records of the court in this particular case as they stand without some explanation will not to my mind help to dissipate the erroneous but nevertheless harmful opinion that many people have of politicians. I submit that no government and no party have the right to allow doubts reflected on the activities of a member of parliament in a transaction which involves the government, and contained in an official document as public as a court judgment, to remain on the records without taking every possible and conceivable means of clarifying all the doubts once and for all, and that not only in the interests of the hon. member for Peel but in the interests and to preserve the prestige and the dignity of parliament and parliamentarians.
I am rather surprised that the Prime Minister and the other members of the government have approached this matter from a rather narrow point of view and that they have so soon forgotten the wonderful speeches they made on how necessary it was to preserve the dignity and the rights of parliament. It appears to me that the true obligation and the true prestige of this house lie not so much in prosecuting or condemning an hon. member as in not allowing anything at all to impair the dignity and the prestige of parliament and that we should do all we can to safeguard and, indeed, to enhance and increase the confidence and the faith of Canadians in parliament and in parliamentarians.
I feel that the Prime Minister's attitude and decision with respect to this matter have all along been contrary to the best interests of parliament and, indeed, contrary to the best interests of the hon. member for Peel. From the moment the Leader of the Opposition questioned the Prime Minister on these important matters concerning the judgment of

the court the house has witnessed the full scope of the Prime Minister's parliamentary tactics, but we have not obtained one solitary piece of information concerning the point at issue. In answer to the Leader of the Opposition's first questions on the matter the Prime Minister replied with what I considered to be one of the finest examples of the Prime Minister's doubletalk in which, of course, he said nothing and meant much less.
What are you quoting from?
Then the Prime Minister tried soft soap-
Would you permit a question, please? You spoke about the Prime Minister's doubletalk. Will you give the exact reference?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Are you asking a question or making a statement?

You are not quoting anything. You are making a ridiculous statement.

Then, Mr. Speaker, when the doubletalk did not work the Prime Minister tried the soft soap method along with the cunning smile we know so well and the sly references. But even that did not work so he tried the old method of trying to divert the attention of the house from the main topic by attacking the opposition and by also introducing a procedural harangue. Finally, the Prime Minister resorted to the more natural characteristic of his government, that of utilizing an appalling amount of arrogance smothered in sanctimony. Incredible as it may seem, the government in the space of two short years has achieved a degree of domineering arrogance that the Liberals could not possibly have acquired in 100 years.
I think the hon. member does not understand the words he is saying.

speechtext: He understands much better than you do.

Not only has the house not yet received any information or any clarification with respect to a transaction which from the judgment of the court itself one could consider as irregular but it is still the intention of the Prime Minister not to give
Malton Land Expropriation members of the house any information on this important and dubious question now before us.
That is not true.

The result is that a comparatively simple problem, which could have been cleared up long ago by an adequate statement from the Prime Minister, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) or even the hon. member for Peel, has turned into something much more important and much more serious-
A witch hunt.

-than the statement of the court with which we are now concerned. The question now is, what does parliament do with a government having an overwhelming majority which absolutely refuses to have a proper inquiry made into statements of a court of justice which imply irregularity on the part of a government member in a transaction in which the government is involved and which cries out for explanation and clarification? There is only one thing that can be done about this matter and I am sure that Canadians will not miss the opportunity of doing so at the next federal election.
Oh, oh.
That is what you are working for, eh?
We are asking that justice be done.
Tell us about Gimli airport.

In spite of the statement made by the hon. member for Peel, for whom I have the greatest respect and, indeed, the greatest of friendship, I would feel that the reasons that he gave for not participating sooner in this debate were a little weak. I believe I am on far firmer ground when I say that, and I am far closer to the truth if I say that I think the hon. member for Peel received instructions not to take part in the debate prior to this time and to forgo the opportunity to speak on his own behalf.
Strictly supposition on your part.

Perhaps, but the supposition I am making now is certainly as strong as the statement the hon. member made a while ago. I may say, Mr. Speaker, that it seems strange to me that the hon. member would not take the opportunity of answering the doubts which, as other hon. members on this side of the house have stated, arise not from the Liberal opposition but from statements

What doubts?

Indeed, if the house is now faced with a motion of non-confidence it is because the opposition felt that the hon. member for Peel should have the opportunity of answering and clarifying these charges.
What charges?

The insinuations that are
contained-
The insinuations you made.
-in the court judgment.
