The insinuations you people over there are making.
"Insinuation" is right.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is not what the Speaker decided. You had better read the judgment.
He used the right word when he said "insinuations".
Who, the Speaker?

I also feel that action on the part of the government aimed at clarifying the situation was called for, not only by the ordinary elementary rules of decency and justice toward an hon. member of the house but by our unanimous dedication to preserve the dignity of parliament and the rights and privileges of its members.
What value can we now place on the many pages of Hansard which the Prime Minister has filled with resounding verbiage as to the necessity of preserving the prestige and rights of parliament, in the face of his decision not to allow an inquiry which would achieve that aim, and the absence of which is detrimental to the dignity of parliament?
Did the Prime Minister really believe that the judgment of the exchequer court, which we now have before us, was the type of document which would add prestige and dignity to parliament? Did the Prime Minister think that he was adding to the rights and privileges of hon. members in this house when by his decision and his attitude he effectively denied the right of a member of parliament to answer on his own behalf, to give his side of the story about the matter mentioned in the court judgment? After all, he was a witness in the case. There is no doubt that the Prime Minister has retreated, and not gracefully at that, from his responsibilities to the house and to parliament in connection with this whole matter ever since it has been brought before the house.

I must say I was quite surprised indeed to read an article in the Saturday Gazette by Mr. Blakely, the headline of which read, "Prime Minister Opens Way for Pallett Debate". One could possibly get the impression from that headline that the Prime Minister was quite anxious to have this particular debate in which we might be able to clarify so many questions which are now so unclear. To anyone who has been following what has been going on in this house in connection with this subject, nothing could be further from the truth. I would have thought that a headline which would have been more in keeping with the facts would have read something like this: "Prime Minister Shamed by Liberals into Opening Way for Pallett Debate". Even this, Mr. Speaker, would not be quite true because the Prime Minister did not open the way to the debating of this question. The way was already open to members of the opposition by the rules and regulations of this house to which Your Honour himself referred before the Prime Minister spoke on this matter. It was only after second thoughts, after realizing the opposition did have an opportunity of debating this question, that the Prime Minister thought he could be magnanimous about it and let the opposition debate the question, to which they had every right according to the rules.
"Prime Minister Opens Way for Pallett Debate". I only wish, Mr. Speaker, I could be so favourably understood and so well interpreted in statements by members of the press gallery as was the Prime Minister in this very difficult situation. There is no doubt but that Mr. Blakely must certainly have been working under a very serious handicap in order to be able to arrive at that particular conclusion. Of course we in the opposition are not so unrealistic as to expect to be interpreted by members of the press gallery on the basis of the very small print that may or may not exist; we of the opposition would be very happy indeed, and very content if they would just write down what we say. With all respect for Mr. Blakely's opinion, I am still convinced that the Prime Minister did not open the way to the Pallett debate.
As a matter of fact, there has been a marked reluctance on the part of the Prime Minister in connection with this matter, not in order to accuse or condemn or punish the hon. member for Peel but to take the necessary steps to clarify this matter by allowing the hon. member to speak on his own behalf to dispel, if possible, any doubt that might have been created by the judgment. Indeed, this procedure would have let the people of Canada know that parliament does have the power to investigate and to stop practices

that are not in the interests of parliament or the people. It is this reluctance, and the not too subtle use of the procedural technique by the Prime Minister to thwart the opposition in its attempt to clarify this matter which might easily lead us to believe that the government has something more serious to hide than what is contained in the court judgment.
Nor does it require much imagination to suspect that the hon. member for Peel might well be the victim of irregularities which stem far more from the partisan policies and practices of this government than they do from the hon. member himself. Has not the Prime Minister in his decision not to clarify this matter chosen to jeopardize, not only the dignity of parliament and the rights of parliamentarians but the reputation and career of one of his best members in order to save the face of the Conservative party?
That is not true, and you know it.

No matter how much hon. gentlemen opposite may protest, these questions are at the root of the problem that faces the house today. If the Prime Minister continues to refuse to clarify this matter, the answers to these questions will be in the affirmative. We will be justified in claiming that just as the government placed the interests of the Conservative party ahead of the economic stability of this country, as is exemplified by the huge deficit this year, so too they do not hesitate now to place the prestige of their political party before the prestige and dignity of parliament, before the rights and privileges of parliamentarians and even, Mr. Speaker, before the elementary principle of justice and decency toward a fellow Canadian, a colleague in this house, the hon. member for Peel, a living victim to the Conservative sacred cow.

Mr. Speaker, there is an amendment to the motion to go into supply now before the house. It was moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) in these terms:
In view of the reasons for judgment of Mr. Justice Thorson in a case concerning the expropriation by the crown of property at Malton, Ontario, and contained in sessional paper 237, a select committee be appointed immediately to investigate and report on all matters connected with this expropriation.
Malton Land Expropriation
Since the Leader of the Opposition has made his very excellent speech outlining in a fair manner all the aspects of this case as set out in the judgment of Mr. Justice Thorson, the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Pallett) has risen to make a statement. As the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) has said, it is unfortunate that the hon. member did not take advantage of the right which he had heretofore to make that statement. While he said that he was unable to speak and felt that he was in a difficult position because of an earlier debate, still we all know in this house that the hon. member could have risen and could have made a statement on a question of privilege or even in the earlier debate. However, he made a statement today and in so far as I am concerned as a member of this house I accept the statement which the hon. member has made. I do not think any member in the house, if he understands his rights, privileges and obligations-and I am sure all of us do- would for one moment not wish to accept the word of an hon. member who rises in his place and says, "Here are the facts as I see them".
None the less, Mr. Speaker, in view of the motion which is before us it is still open to hon. members on this side of the house to place before you and the house, in speaking to this amendment, some of the difficulties which still lie in the way. I propose to do that and I hope that in the course of the intervention which I shall make I shall say nothing which will in the slightest degree be unjust or unfair to the hon. member. However, I want at once to indicate to you, Mr. Speaker and to the house, the entirely different attitude taken by the other side of the house in this debate from that taken in the earlier debate. I want to point out that at least in this debate we were listened to with attention and with care and were followed in the interventions which we attempted to make. That was not the situation on the earlier occasion.
On the earlier occasion we were attacked for lacking courage, being guilty of McCarthyism, being guilty of making innuendos and insinuations and the like. What has been the reason for the change in the attitude of hon. members opposite? Is it because of statements contained in the press? Is it because the government has begun to realize that there was something in the attitude of the opposition which asked for an explanation of the contradictions which existed? Be that as it may, I note with a great deal of satisfaction the change in the attitude in this debate compared with that in the earlier debate.

I say that the object of this amendment is to revive a matter which we tried unsuccessfully to bring before the house on a matter of privilege. We tried unsuccessfully to do it in a motion which was placed on the order paper by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) and on which you, Mr. Speaker, ruled in a fairly lengthy judgment. I have no fault to find with that judgment. Indeed, I submit to the ruling of the Chair which is also, because of the appeal to the house, the decision of the house. It seems to me that a supply motion is neither the time nor the place to discuss a matter of this kind. In my opinion a supply motion is the time to deal with matters concerning the non-confidence which the opposition has in the government. I want to say here that this occasion provides me with an opportunity to make some comments in connection with the rights of the opposition in this house concerning the use of supply days. On more than one occasion it has been indicated in this house by the government that we should use supply days for certain debates.
It is your choice, not ours.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Just a minute. The opposition is entitled to six supply days. They are set aside in the standing orders in order to permit the opposition, on motions to go into supply, to move amendments of non-confidence against the government. Surely, Mr. Speaker, what the opposition does on these motions, what subjects it chooses to debate, are prerogatives of the opposition, not of the government, and should be protected. There has been in this house when we move the adjournment of the house to discuss a matter of urgent public importance an increasing practice to suggest "Oh, the matter is not important enough; we will give you the opportunity of discussing it on a supply motion on Monday". On two occasions when, from this side, we moved the adjournment of the house in order to discuss a matter of urgent public importance the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) rose-and I believe also the leader of the house-to say that this was a matter which need not be debated now but which should be debated on a supply motion, and immediately he said "I make that opportunity available". As Your Honour knows full well, the rule sets out clearly what are the reasons for the adjournment of the house on a matter of urgent public


importance. The fact that there is going to be a supply motion is not one of those reasons. I therefore deprecate the attitude which is being adopted by the government and on the other side of the house in attempting to curtail the rights of discussion of the opposition by saying to them from time to time, "Oh, you are going to have a supply motion on Monday; raise the matter on that occasion". That procedure I say is an infringement upon the rights of the opposition and places an unfair limitation upon our freedom of action in moving supply amendments.
I should like now to pass on to another consideration in this matter. Why do we find ourselves today discussing this matter? Why do we find ourselves in effect discussing a matter of privilege on a want of confidence motion?
That is the $64 question.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned at six o'clock I was discussing the so-called Foster case, and I had put on record certain of the statements made by Sir Robert Borden. I think I can summarize the whole thing very quickly, and I am sure Your Honour will not be displeased at my decision so to do, by simply stating that in his summation of the report in connection with Foster, Sir Robert Borden at no point said that Mr. Foster had acted for his private gain or had been guilty of moral wrongdoing. Then Sir Robert went on to say:
I am not concerned about Mr. Garland; I am concerned about Mr. Foster. He Is not shown to have profited in any way by the transaction. He is a very young man, altogether inexperienced in business. What he tried to do was to try to get more money for the horses of his constituents.
The parallel I want to draw here is that what the hon. member for Peel tried to do was to get more money for the land of his constituents than the president of the exchequer court thought it was worth. So that there is a parallel to be drawn between these two cases. In the case of Mr. Foster, the so-called Foster-Garland case, there was no hesitation on the part of Sir Robert Borden in suggesting that the matter be sent to a committee notwithstanding that it was found therein that there was no moral wrongdoing in the case. I thought I should bring that to your attention.
The hon. member for Peel put on record what had been said by Mr. Burke in connection with the duties and responsibilities of a member of parliament, and I would like to put on the record also what one finds concerning that matter in Beauchesne's third edition, citation 20, page 11, which reads as follows:
Every member as soon as he is chosen becomes a representative of the whole body of the Commons, without any distinction of the place from whence he is sent to parliament. . . . that every member is equally a representative of the whole has been the constant notion and language of parliament. Every member, though chosen by one particular district, when elected and returned, serves for the whole realm.
So in view of this citation, in view of the statement of the hon. member for Peel, and in


view of the refusal of the Minister of Transport to make a statement, which I am sure the house would welcome, in order to clear up some of the contradictions, I should like to ask the Prime Minister who is now in his seat these questions. Does a member who unsuccessfully attempts to get funds from the public treasury for his constituents, which they do not deserve, serve in the public interest? Has parliament now decided that a member can with propriety and without any breach of the privileges of parliament go out and seek for his constituents funds from the public treasury which in the circumstances they are not warranted in having? Does a member who seeks to bind the crown by the imposition of valuations which were not in accordance with the actual and true market value of the land serve in the public interest? Has parliament now decided that a member can with propriety and without any breach of the privileges of parliament seek unduly to increase the actual or fair market value of land? Does a member who himself obtains from the valuator the valuations themselves contrary to the practice of the Department of Transport and then turns them over to the minister's executive assistant serve in the public interest? Has parliament now decided that a member can with propriety and without any breach of the privileges of the house act in this manner? Those, it seems to me, without in any way prejudging in any way what has been said by anyone who has taken part in the debate, are some of the questions which in the light of what has taken place in this and the other debate demand clarification on the part of the government.
Now may I turn to another matter which is also germane to the issue and it is this. It is amazing to me that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) has seen fit not to take part in this discussion. Here is a motion of non-confidence. It is a motion of nonconfidence in the government affecting the Department of Transport, affecting the officers of the Department of Transport, affecting a member of parliament in so far as his relations are concerned with the Department of Transport, and the minister has seen fit not to say anything. He chooses to say nothing in this debate. He says that he cannot be expected to discuss the judgment. The judgment is not in appeal; the judgment is not sub judice. There are many of us who have discussed the judgment: the Leader of the Opposition at great length; the member for Bonavista-Twillingate; the member for Essex East (Mr. Martin); the member himself who is concerned made certain statements in connection with it; the Prime Minister; and also, I believe, the Minister of Justice. All of them

saw fit to discuss the judgment, and still the Minister of Transport whose department is most vitally interested and certainly closely concerned has seen fit not to rise and take part in this discussion.
Why did the minister appoint the valuator Clare who turned out to be anything but an independent valuator? I think the minister owes it to this house to explain some of the contradictions that are to be found in the judgment. The hon. member for Peel in his explanation earlier in the day said there was a simple misunderstanding between himself and the minister. It seems to me that it is incumbent upon the minister to rise and clear up this misunderstanding. When did the minister tell the hon. member for Peel that he was mistaken? He said that he did not go to court because he was not subpoenaed. Everybody knows that that is no reason for not going to court. One has not necessarily to be subpoenaed in order to go to court. There were a number of contradictions affecting the minister, affecting a member of parliament and affecting officers of the Department of Transport, and still the minister saw fit not to clear up those contradictions. He might well have done so by going voluntarily to court.
I wonder if the hon. members would permit a question. He says it is not necessary to be subpoenaed. Would the hon. member suggest that a person could take the witness box by force?

Mr. Speaker, dealing first of all with what the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) has just said, I have this to say. I have no recollection of any conversation regarding the Malton valuations with a Mr. White. The conversation he describes did not take place between me and anyone else at any time. It would have been impossible for me to make the statements attributed to me by Mr. White for the following reasons: First, there never was any agreement that the valuations made by Mr. Clare would be accepted by the department and therefore it would have been impossible for me to refer

to any agreements. Second, I signed no valuations for submission to treasury board and no other documents, purposed by Mr. White to be agreements, for submission to the treasury board. Third, there never was any intention or indication of intention to have these valuations submitted to treasury board for consideration before they had been examined by the treasury board staff. This staff has had great experience in examining real estate values.
Had the treasury board staff been able to show that the new valuations were correct I would have submitted them to treasury board in place of the valuations previously submitted by the department. This, however, did not happen. Fourth, it is impossible for any minister of the crown to give assurance that payments will be made until those payments have first been authorized by treasury board. If Mr. White really believes the statement he has made it seems strange indeed that he did not arrange to be called as a witness before the exchequer court when the Drew case was being heard as I believe he has been closely associated with this case for some time.
Maybe he was not subpoenaed.

Mr. Speaker, as I said in the house, in my dealings with the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Pallett) on the question of these valuations it was clear to me that he felt strongly that the previous valuations of these properties were too low and therefore were unfair to his constituents. I am convinced that his interest in this whole matter was to make sure that a fair valuation was placed on these properties. That, I feel, is the duty of every member of parliament in serving those he represents.
I agreed completely with the hon. member for Peel in believing that the misunderstanding regarding acceptance of the Clare valuations by the department may have arisen in the following way. I assured the hon. member for Peel that Mr. Clare's valuations would be submitted to the treasury board staff for examination. He may have understood, and he has said that he did, that the submission was to be to the treasury board itself in which case valuations would have gone forward over my signature indicating acceptance of them by the department. As he has indicated this afternoon, this misunderstanding occurred very naturally over the terms "treasury board" and "treasury board staff".
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) asked me three questions this afternoon which he did not give me a chance to answer and I am very glad to answer them now.

You have a chance now.

First of all, I was asked why an independent evaluator was named. The hon. member for Peel came to me shortly after we formed the government in June of 1957. He told me that for several years he had been working on behalf of a group of people in the Malton district who felt that the valuations which had been put on their properties by the Department of Transport were too low and therefore were unfair; that he had brought this matter to the attention of the former government and had got nowhere at all with them and that he felt very strongly about the matter. He asked me to help him to find out whether or not these valuations were fair, and he believed very strongly that they were not. So, because this government is interested in helping the little people, the small people, the people who are normally pushed around by bureaucrats and who were pushed around by the former autocratic government which had been in power a great length of time and obviously cared nothing for the welfare of little people-
How about Mr. White?
-and because this government believes it should go to every practical and possible length to make sure that the little people of this country-
That the little people are fooled.
-receive a square deal and do not get pushed around, for that reason I agreed to the appointment of an independent valuator.
Knowing you would not take his valuation.
A Tory organizer.

I did so to find out if there was anything he could bring to light which would indicate clearly that the previous valuations had been too low and were unfair, and I agreed that I would submit these valuations for scrutiny by an independent group experienced in examining real estate valuations because they examine a great many during a year submitted to them by all departments, that independent group being the treasury board staff.
The independent valuator, Mr. Clare, was appointed after the department satisfied itself that his qualifications were satisfactory and I enunciated those qualifications in the House of Commons when I was speaking on my estimates a week ago last Thursday. When Mr. Clare turned in his valuations for these properties they were submitted to the treasury board staff for examination and the result of that examination was that they believed that the valuations were too high, were not correct

Malton Land Expropriation and could not be supported, and for that reason they were not submitted by me to treasury board for their approval. The matter then went to the exchequer court, which is the correct procedure when there is a dispute that cannot be settled in this way.
That should have been done in the first place.

That deals with the first question, why was an independent evaluator appointed. Second, the Leader of the Opposition asked me why we attempted to bind the property owners only. The answer is that six valuations had been made by evaluators working for the Department of Transport and none of those evaluations had been accepted by the small group of home owners in question, even though a very large number of home owners in the area had accepted those evaluations. The department wanted to make sure that if the study by the treasury board staff indicated that these evaluations were correct, the evaluations submitted by Mr. Clare were correct and should be submitted to the treasury board for approval, and if the treasury board passed these evaluations, then this long drawn out matter could be virtually concluded.
The hon. Leader of the Opposition asked why we did not attempt to bind both the government and the property owners. The answer is obvious. It is impossible to bind the government in a matter of this kind, and he knows it quite well. But in an attempt to bring an end to this matter which had been started by the government of which the Leader of the Opposition was a member and which had dragged out for some years, and since there had been five or six evaluations previously which had not been accepted, it was thought this was the best way to bring the matter to a culmination.
Then, third, he has asked me, why did I not correct the misunderstanding in the mind of the hon. member for Peel? The answer is that I believed that he understood the basis upon which we were working while these evaluations were made, and of course when the evaluations were turned down by treasury board staff, then the whole matter was well known. I believe that concludes the questions which the Leader of the Opposition and others have asked me, including the hon. member for Trinity. I assume that disposes of the matter they have tried to raise.
In conclusion, I simply want to say this.

The most important question was, why he did not inform these people, the little people, before they went to the court that there had been a misunderstanding? not getting a square deal, and he did everything possible to see that they got a square deal; no more and no less, and that is the duty of every good member of parliament. My whole purpose in having a further evaluation made was to see if, in the past, there was anything to indicate the valuators had erred or done an injustice to the small people of Canada, the people in the hon. member for Peel's riding, the people who needed to have somebody stand up and fight their battles for them, something the Leader of the Opposition does not seem to understand. The resolution in the name of the Minister of Agriculture indicates that for the first time some supervised loans might be developed. Is there going to be economy; is there going to be some kind of co-ordination, because I am satisfied that the same number of civil servants-and they are very capable -that we now have in the Department of Veterans Affairs supervising Veterans' Land Act loans of about $90 million to $100 million could take on an additional $100 million without any increase in over-all civil service staff. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in view of the discussion we had on second reading and the very thorough discussion of this bill and the consideration that was given it by the committee on veterans affairs, I do not think there is any necessity to speak on the first clause. I think I shall deal with the suggestions we have to make when we reach the various clauses in question. However, I do want to say, Mr. Chairman, that the members of the committee, after examining the administration officials of the Veterans' Land Act and other witnesses, were more than ever impressed with the excellent work being done by this administration and particularly with the, shall I say, supervised credit aspects of the administration which, in the opinion of the committee as a whole, regardless of party membership, sets a model for other agriculture credit legislation. Not only did the committee report unanimously, but so did also the representatives of the Canadian Legion. I just want to quote briefly from their submission to the committee as presented by Mr. D. M. Thompson, director of the service bureau, in respect of this bill. In this brief I read:
The Canadian Legion welcomes this opportunity to appear before the committee concerning Bill C-50.
We would, first of all, like to commend the introduction of this bill. We believe that the benefits of the Veterans' Land Act have been invaluable to those veterans established under this legislation, but this bill will make it even more valuable and will

encourage many more to participate. We also want to express our appreciation to the director, and his staff for the excellent work that they have done down through the years to ensure that the full spirit of the Veterans' Land Act legislation has been met. They deserve a great deal of credit for the success of veteran farmers.
I might say that when this portion of the brief was read it was received with applause from all members of the committee.
The Legion did make a few suggestions with respect to amendments to this bill. They suggested that clause 15, which sets a ceiling of $10,000 on loans, should perhaps be increased to $10,500 to provide what they termed a slight cushion for increases which would probably occur between now and the next amending of the act. The committee discussed this matter and realized the Legion's intention in this respect, but did not see fit at the time to recommend this increase in the amount in clause 15.
Then, with respect to clause 20, they made further representations to increase the amount from $20,000 to $25,000. The committee discussed this recommendation quite thoroughly and with sympathy and I think it is fair to say that generally they came to the conclusion that, in view of the amount being raised to $25,000, they would be making a good step in that direction and possibly the experience of the years ahead would give us further ground for asking for the increase the Legion asked for in this section.
Mr. Chairman, that is all I have to say . at this time except in conclusion to say that, like other members of the committee-and I think this was generally expressed in the committee-we all hope that the new agricultural credit legislation to be introduced by the government will be patterned to quite an extent on the Veterans' Land Act legislation and that it will make provision for supervised credit. I want to say frankly, Mr. Chairman, it is the opinion of this group that with respect to the supervision of agricultural credit for other than farmer veterans we could not do better than utilize the trained personnel of the Veterans' Land Act administration.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO PROVIDE FURTHER ASSISTANCE FOR HOME CONSTRUCTION, TO FARMERS AND FISHERMEN, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks regarding this legislation. In the first place, may I say that since I came to the House of Commons I have never seen a more efficient brief presented to a committee than that presented by the director of the Veterans' Land Act administration. I am disappointed that the legislation regarding extended mortgage credit to farmers has not been introduced by the Minister of Agriculture. If that legislation had been brought down before continuing consideration of this legislation I think we would

have been in a position to discuss the matter much more intelligently than we are at the present time because we are in the dark as to what the legislation to be brought forward by the Minister of Agriculture really contains. For that reason I am more or less at a loss because I would have liked to be able to discuss this legislation on the basis of knowledge of what the other contains. As the director stated in his very excellent brief:
By far the most important amendment proposed in this bill is the one providing for a very substantial increase in the part III loans available to veterans certified to be qualified as full-time farmers, and who are now, or who may be in the future, settled under part I of the act.
The definition of a family farm unit given by the director was accepted by the committee. He said that a family farm unit is an organized assembly of farm lands, farm buildings, livestock and equipment which can be managed and operated by the owner and his family and which, under his management, will produce enough net income to pay three-quarters of its cost with interest amortized over a period of 30 years, pay the cost of good maintenance, and leave enough to supply the farmer and his immediate family with a typical Canadian standard of living. The members of the committee agreed that the original loan ceiling of $6,000 to a full-time veteran farmer was entirely inadequate, and I do not think any member of the committee would disagree with that statement. Many of us were prepared to raise the ceiling to $25,000 but the amount agreed upon ultimately was $20,000 which I believe will be sufficient in the majority of cases. I expect that the new legislation to be brought forward by the Minister of Agriculture will have a ceiling of $20,000 as well.
The experience of the government with the Soldier Settlement Act was a very unhappy one, as we all know, and probably that is why we made haste slowly in the development of a satisfactory ceiling under the Veterans' Land Act. The Veterans' Land Act is terminable legislation. The Canadian farm loan board is self-sustaining and has been since its inception.

speechtext: It even pays income tax.

speechtext:
Veterans' Land Act
which will afford the farmer and his family a good living and at the same time maintain and pay for itself. We have the word of the director that such credit men are very hard to come by.
Out of 76,000 veterans settled under part I of the act, that is, full-time farmers, only 182 have had to be put off their properties for one reason or another. Although collections amount to over $20 million a year, under $12,000 remains due and owing over three years. This is a remarkable achievement. Full-time farmers under the Veterans' Land Act are being well served. As I said, loans under the act are showing a steady decline as is to be expected and before too long the Veterans' Land Act appraisers and supervisers will be compelled to seek other employment unless jobs are found for them. It has been shown that the important people in the Veterans' Land Act organization are the people on the ground, that is, the appraisers, supervisers and credit men.
The director stated that his men are well trained and experienced in assisting farmers to prepare plans for the organization and operation of their units. He pointed out that much of their time is spent on this and in going with the farmer to visit successful and well organized operations. In the final analysis, the director said, the plan must be the farmer's own and completely acceptable to him because he is the man who has to make it work.
If these highly trained officials were not available the administration of the Veterans' Land Act would be seriously handicapped. So, Mr. Chairman, the administration now has a staff of highly trained men who can not only handle the additional work brought about by the extra farm credit set forth in the amendment of the Veterans' Land Act but can, I believe, take over the appraisal and field work required in the administration of the new legislation about to be enacted and also in connection with the Farm Improvement Loans Act. The director of the Veterans' Land Act administration assured the committee that he not only had a highly qualified administrative staff but a very capable group of appraisers and credit advisers. He further stated, and this is significant, that without this efficient organization he would not be prepared to recommend the type of credit legislation introduced by this amendment which raises the permissible amount of the loan for a full-time farmer to $20,000. In speaking at Edmonton last year the Minister of Veterans Affairs said:
Undoubtedly a good deal of the credit for this fine record belongs to the Veterans' Land Act field supervisors who have become experts in advising the settlers on how to use their resources to the best advantage in order to neutralize, to some
[Mr. Forgie.l
extent at least, any unfavourable prices for farm products. The Veterans Land Act officials are presently engaged in a survey to determine what is needed to improve the incomes of our full-time farmers. So far they have analysed reports on the farm business of over 3,000 settlers and have found that the key to the problem for most of them is more capital. The survey is continuing, and we are studying the possibility of making more supervised capital available to these farmers.
I believe that is the statement the minister made. The survey has now been completed on 5,000 farms and a report made to the minister. The present amendments, I am quite satisfied, stem from the reports on these 5,000 farms.
As we know, it is the intention of the administration to repeal the Canadian Farm Loan Act and introduce other legislation. The Canadian farm loan board is short of qualified appraisers and credit advisers such as those possessed by the Veterans' Land Act administration. It was pointed out by the chairman of the Canadian farm loan board that 25 per cent of the loans they have made have been for consolidation of debts, and it may be that there has been a significant increase in loans for this purpose. Many farmers, apart from veteran farmers, really cannot make a go of it because their acreage is too small, the amount of livestock inadequate to operate economically, or they lack farm machinery.
The amendments to the Canadian Farm Loan Act in 1958 did not result in any improvement in conditions prior to the amendments, other than to provide additional funds which will be increased when the Minister of Agriculture introduces his long awaited farm policy and presents legislation necessary to carry into effect the proposed measure for long term mortgage credit. The opinion expressed by the two largest agricultural organizations in Canada is to the effect that, with its present administrative set-up, the Canadian farm loan board cannot base its lending decisions on the intimate knowledge of farming conditions and appraisal of the personal capacities of the borrower which are necessary to a flexible and helpful lending policy. These organizations recommend the setting up of regional advisory committees which could work with the loan board officials. Mortgage and insurance companies can find more lucrative and less risky loans than farm loans, and so the government must find a practical source of credit for our farmers, especially long term credit with reasonable interest rates. At the present time the ceiling for loans under the Canadian Farm Loan Act is $15,000. As we all know, it is expected and I am quite sure it will happen when the new legislation is introduced

that this ceiling will be increased to $20,000 to conform to the provisions of the Veterans' Land Act.

Mr. Chairman, in his opening remarks the minister referred to two amendments which resulted, I think, from an examination of sections 36 and 76 of the act. I believe these two amendments were recommended by the committee. However, there was a discussion of another possible amendment in the committee which revolved around the position of those veterans who have been considered as already established under this act.
These veterans fall into two classes, those who have received their title and those who have continued to leave their title with the Department of Veterans Affairs. It appears
66968-9-3191
Veterans' Land Act
that those who have left their titles with the department, although they are established, are eligible to receive further loans under this act, while those who have accepted their titles are not. A considerable amount of time was given over to the discussion of this point in the committee. Some members felt that when a veteran was established, he was established once and for all and there was no further obligation or commitment to do anything else for him. There were some members who contended that it would be introducing a new principle to establish a veteran twice if he were to receive loans under this act.
There were others, and I was included amongst this second group, who felt that although a veteran had been established it would be the wish of parliament and I am sure of the department that he should remain established. We are all aware of the changing conditions which are taking place so rapidly that a person's income can be affected overnight. If a veteran needed more money to enlarge his operation or to get more modern equipment in order to remain an economic unit we felt he should be entitled to receive it under this act. Since those who had elected to leave their titles with the department appeared to be eligible for this we saw no reason why those who had accepted their titles should be excluded.
There was no definite decision on this matter in the committee, but it was something we hoped the minister and his colleagues would consider favourably in the case of veterans who might need additional assistance, even though they might have been considered to be established. In my opinion it is unfortunate, as other members have pointed out, that this legislation is being dealt with before the new legislation or the new amendments to amend the Canadian Farm Loan Board Act are brought in by the Minister of Agriculture. We do not know what terms will be available to farmers under that piece of legislation. We are all anxious that under this legislation the veteran should at least be treated as generously as the non-veteran under the Canadian Farm Loan Board Act. In the case of the veteran who has already been established, we feel that he would like to remain under the Veterans' Land Act, and we hope that the treatment he will receive under this legislation will at least be the same as that which he would receive under the Canadian Farm Loan Board Act.

Mr. Speaker, tomorrow we will continue consideration in committee of Bill No. C-62 which we have just been discussing followed by the second reading of Bill No. C-61, an act to authorize the provision of money to meet certain capital expenditures of the C.N.R.; then take second reading of Bill No. C-63, an act to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act; then take second reading of Bill No. C-60, an act respecting the adjustment of certain public service pensions; then take item No. 10 on today's order paper, the second reading of Bill No.
C-57, an act respecting the superannuation of members of the R.C.M.P.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Items Nos. 10 and 3 will be reversed; No. 3 will come before No. 10.

That is correct. Arrangements have been made for item No. 3 to be taken before item No. 10. Item No. 3 on today's order paper relates to committee consideration of Bill No. C-34, an act respecting the R.C.M.P.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: What shall we do on Wednesday and Thursday?
If we get through with all these bills tomorrow, on Wednesday we will go on with-

At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
The following answers, deposited with the Clerk of the house, are printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

1.	Has the Prime Minister received representations protesting against the most recent order in council limiting immigration in Canada?
2.	If so, what reply has been made to these representations by the Prime Minister?
Answer by: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker
(Prime Minister):
1.	Yes. Three communications were received.
2.	The representations were carefully noted and they were sent to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.

1.	Did the Indian government request a Canadian expert to produce visual aids needed for Colombo plan projects to assist in the development of Indian villages?
2.	If so, when was this request made of the Canadian government?
3.	Has the request been met? If so, when?
Answer by: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister
of Trade and Commerce):
1.	The government of India requested Canada to provide the services of a technical expert in film making to advise the reserve bank of India on the production of cooperative training films to be produced in India and distributed through the various co-operative training centres in the country. The services of the expert were requested in conjunction with another request for film raw stock with which to make the training films.
2.	This request was made by the Indian government at the end of August 1958, and received in Ottawa in mid-September 1958.
3.	Some film equipment will be provided when the present negotiations with the Indian government on these matters are completed. Names and qualifications of experts are now under consideration for the production of the films on co-operatives and the training of native staff in their use.

1.	Was dredging authorized for East Petpeswick, Nova Scotia, during the past 12 months?
2.	If authorized and completed, was the work performed found satisfactory by the department and by the fishermen who operate boats making use of this port?
3.	Was the work performed under contract or by government equipment and crew?
4.	If by government equipment, how many days work by the dredge and crew were required to complete this work?
5.	Was there any lost time when the dredge was inoperative during the period of operations? If so, how many days?
6.	What were the following costs (a) total costs; (b) wages; (c) towing; (d) operation of dredge; (e) charges against lost time; (f) costs of feeding and housing crew?
Answer by: Hon. Howard C. Green (Minister
of Public Works):
1.	Yes.
2.	Yes, in so far as the department is aware.
3.	By government equipment and crew.
4.	41 calendar days.
5.	(a) Yes; (b) 26 days. (11 days-Saturdays, Sundays and statutory holidays, 10 days due to bad weather and 5 days for miscellaneous causes.)
6.	(a) Estimated cost, $5,230; (b) wages $3,230; (c) towing, $100; (d) operation of dredge, $735, (not including wages and subsistence); (e) charge against lost time, $725, (not including wages, subsistence and fuel); (f) cost of feeding crew, $440, (accommodation supplied on dredge).

1.	Has an agreement been signed between the federal government and the government of the province of New Brunswick, in connection with the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act?
2.	If not, what is the cause for the delay?
Answer by: Hon. J. W. Monleiih (Minister
of National Health and Welfare):
An agreement under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act has not as yet been signed with the province of New Brunswick. However, discussions preparatory to signing an agreement are proceeding and it is anticipated that an agreement will be signed in the very near future.
